text:
THE ANATOMY OF AI THEFT: Why celebrating unauthorised distillation could eventually hurt all of us.

Some people in the AI community are celebrating the unauthorised distillation of frontier models as a victory for open-source AI and acceleration.

I think they're missing the bigger picture.

Let's break it down.

1. The economics of stealing intelligence

Company A spends billions on infrastructure, compute, research, engineering, training and safety.

Company B extracts capabilities from Company A's proprietary model without authorisation, trains its own model using those outputs and releases it at a fraction of the original development cost.

Distillation itself is perfectly legitimate when authorised. Unauthorised extraction is an entirely different conversation.

If this becomes an accepted business practice, what happens to the financial incentive to develop genuinely new intelligence?

Why spend billions pioneering something when your competitors can simply wait and imitate it?

2. Intelligence without equivalent safeguards

You can transfer capabilities without necessarily transferring the safety mechanisms that govern them.

Advanced reasoning, cybersecurity, autonomous agents, chemistry and biological research are incredibly useful capabilities. They can also be misused.

Imagine these capabilities becoming widely accessible through models with significantly weaker safeguards.

It only takes one major incident for governments to respond with sweeping restrictions that affect everyone.

3. You're strengthening the argument for slowing down AI

This is where the irony becomes almost comical.

People who champion acceleration are inadvertently strengthening the arguments of people like Dario Amodei, who advocate pacing frontier AI development and introducing greater oversight.

Every major unauthorised distillation campaign gives advocates of tighter regulation another piece of evidence.

Every serious security incident gives governments another reason to intervene.

You're practically handing ammunition to the very movement you oppose.

4. The consequences for ordinary consumers

What could happen next?

• Stricter API access and usage limits.
• Mandatory identity verification.
• Higher subscription and API costs.
• More geographical restrictions.
• Tighter chip and cloud-compute export controls.
• Delayed model releases.
• More restrictive open-weight licensing.
• Less transparency from frontier AI laboratories.
• Greater regulatory and legal barriers for smaller AI companies.

None of these outcomes benefits me as a consumer.

And this isn't purely hypothetical anymore. Google, Anthropic and OpenAI have all publicly documented unauthorised distillation attacks and are actively strengthening their defences.

5. The long-term paradox

Unauthorised distillation might accelerate one company's progress in the short term while slowing down the wider industry in the long term.

That's not sustainable acceleration. That's borrowing progress from the future.

I want Chinese AI to succeed. I want American AI to succeed. I want European AI to succeed. I want affordable, powerful open-source models.

But I want genuine competition and responsible innovation.

I'm not defending corporate profits. I'm defending my interests as a consumer.

Because when AI becomes more expensive, more restricted, less accessible or slower to develop, I lose.

And so do you.

Don't confuse technological acceleration with technological recklessness. The former opens doors. The latter gives people reasons to close them.

The phrase "open-source AI" covers very different things, and that is part of what makes this debate difficult.

A small model released by university researchers is not necessarily comparable to a frontier model trained by a company spending hundreds of millions of dollars.

Dario Amodei made this distinction during his 2023 Senate testimony.

He said open source is generally good for scientific progress and that smaller developers iterating quickly should be encouraged.

His concern was about much larger organizations releasing increasingly powerful models without the ability to monitor their future use.

Why does that distinction matter?

Because releasing model weights changes who can use the technology and how much control the original developer retains.

A hosted AI service can introduce restrictions, monitor suspicious activity, and update its model. A downloaded model can be copied, modified, fine-tuned, and redistributed.

The same openness that helps researchers experiment also makes centralized intervention much harder.

That is the actual policy challenge. How do you preserve the benefits of open AI development without ignoring the risks of distributing increasingly capable systems?

text:
Lutnick's One Letter Shut Off Anthropic's Top AI for 18 Days

On Friday, June 12, 2026, at 5:21 PM Eastern, Anthropic ($ANT) received a letter from Howard Lutnick. Lutnick is the Commerce Secretary in President Donald Trump's (R) cabinet and the former chief executive of Wall Street firm Cantor Fitzgerald.

By that night, Anthropic's two newest and most powerful AI models were dark for every customer it had. They stayed dark until June 30.

That is the whole lesson. A closed AI model runs on its owner's servers, so one letter to one company can switch it off. An open-weight model sitting on your own computer has no switch in Washington.

WHAT THE LETTER SAID

The letter went to Dario Amodei, Anthropic's co-founder and chief executive. It required an export license before Anthropic could release Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Fable 5 to any foreign national, inside or outside the United States.

That included Anthropic's own employees who are not American citizens.

Anthropic had launched both models three days earlier, on Tuesday, June 9. They share one underlying model.

Fable was the public version with heavy safety filters. Mythos had fewer filters and went only to a small group of partners doing defensive cybersecurity work.

Anthropic had no way to check a user's citizenship in real time. So it pulled both models from everyone, American or not.

A license requirement aimed at foreigners became a shutdown for the whole country.

WHY COMMERCE PULLED THE PLUG

The trigger was a report by researchers at Amazon ($AMZN). They found a way to prompt Fable 5 into listing software vulnerabilities, and in one case it wrote code showing how to exploit one.

Anthropic then ran the same test on other models. Its own older Claude models found the same flaws, and so did GPT-5.5 from OpenAI. So did Kimi K2.7, an open-weight model from Moonshot AI in Beijing, China.

When it came to writing the exploit code, every model Anthropic tested could do it.

So the American model went dark, and the Chinese model that could do the same job kept running on any machine that had downloaded it. No letter from Commerce could reach that one.

Anthropic called the order a "misunderstanding." It said a narrow workaround to its filters was no reason to recall a model "deployed to hundreds of millions of people," and warned that the same standard "would essentially halt all new model deployments for all frontier model providers."

A LAW NOBODY HAD USED

Lutnick reached for the Export Control Reform Act of 2018, which Trump signed in his first term. That law lets Commerce put temporary controls on "emerging and foundational technologies" and notify a company by letter that it needs a license.

Congress told Commerce to write regulations spelling out how that power works. Commerce never wrote them.

That is why the power had never been used as the basis for a control before June 12. The first time it was used, it hit a single American company's flagship product worldwide.

The letter also cited a rule that lets Commerce block exports headed for foreign military intelligence. That rule normally covers a short list of hostile countries. This letter covered every foreign person on the planet.

THE PRICE OF GETTING IT BACK

On June 26, Commerce let Mythos 5 return, but only for a set of approved U.S. organizations.

On June 30, Lutnick sent a second letter lifting the license requirement. This one went to Tom Brown, an Anthropic co-founder and its chief compute officer, not to Amodei.

The letter spelled out what Anthropic agreed to. It will "proactively detect and address security risks" in the models. It will work with the government "on protocols and standards and releases for Mythos, Fable, and future models."

And it will "inform the U.S. government of any malicious activity."

Read that last line twice. The company that runs the model now tells the government when it spots malicious use.

Fable 5 came back on July 1. The final paragraph of Lutnick's letter kept the switch loaded: Commerce "reserves the right" to bring the license requirement back "should circumstances change or should Anthropic fail to adhere to its commitments."

The off switch was never removed. It was set back on the wall.

"WE TRUST ANTHROPIC"

On September 2, Axios co-founder Mike Allen asked Lutnick whether he trusts Amodei.

Lutnick answered, "We trust Anthropic. They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side."

He said it in Chapel Hill, North Carolina, at the G20 Innovation Ministerial, a meeting of technology ministers from the world's 20 largest economies. That week he introduced Brown to the room.

"They've done what we asked" is the whole arrangement in five words. Trust came after compliance, and the compliance included a promise to report malicious activity to the government.

The Pentagon didn't go along. The day after Lutnick spoke, Emil Michael, the Pentagon's under secretary for research and engineering, posted that Anthropic was "still a designated Supply Chain Risk" for the Department of War and its contractors.

The Pentagon had slapped that label on Anthropic in March after the company refused to let the military use its models for mass surveillance of Americans or fully autonomous weapons.

A federal judge struck the designation down in August, ruling that the government had punished Anthropic for speaking out. Anthropic is still fighting a second designation in the federal appeals court in Washington.

THE PROMISE ABOUT OPEN MODELS

In July 2025, the White House published America's AI Action Plan. One heading reads "Encourage Open-Source and Open-Weight AI."

An open-weight model is one whose trained numbers are published, so anyone can download it and run it on their own hardware. The plan said these models "have unique value for innovation because startups can use them flexibly without being dependent on a closed model provider." It said "the Federal government should create a supportive environment for open models."

June 12 showed exactly what being dependent on a closed model provider means. Every customer using Fable 5 lost it overnight, on a letter none of them ever saw.

Six weeks later, on July 24, 2026, Jensen Huang, the co-founder and chief executive of Nvidia ($NVDA), put out a public letter titled "Open Weights and American AI Leadership." It warned that closed models "can be breached, misused, or fail in ways that outsiders cannot detect." It asked Washington to avoid "premature restrictions on open models."

Anthropic, the lab Lutnick had just switched off, is missing from its signer list. Three days later Amodei wrote that "Anthropic has never advocated for a ban on open-weights models," while calling for mandatory safety testing of the most capable ones.

REPORT AND YOU MAY PASS

On November 16, Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, the office that runs export controls, issued an interim rule on remote access to advanced chips. Its press release said the rule was written "by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council."

The rule adds a new license requirement for advanced chips shipped to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.

That new license "will not apply to semiconductors destined to companies headquartered in" the United States, "provided certain reporting requirements are met." The exemption covers that one new license and nothing wider. Every other chip license stands.

Look at the pattern. Anthropic got its models back by agreeing to report. American chip buyers get past the new license by agreeing to report. In 2026, reporting to Washington is the price of access.

THE JAIL LINE

On November 8, CBS aired a 60 Minutes interview with Trump. He said the risk from AI "can be managed, and it's managed," and credited the Justice Department.

Then he gave an example.

"We had a situation where somebody was reported to us to be doing something bad with AI. We called them very strongly and said, 'Get ready to go to jail. Please give your wife a kiss good night.'"

He would not name the person or the company. He said it was the leader of an AI company, "one of the big ones," and that after the threat, "this person totally changed everything."

The President of the United States said on national television that a phone call threatening prison made the leader of a major AI company change everything. No court was involved in that call.

THE SAME HAND ON NVIDIA

Four days after that interview, Huang was out at Nvidia. On November 23, the board put him back as president, chief executive and director.

The board's own statement said it "received input from senior levels of the United States government." Based on that input, it was "confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."

Anthropic's best models came back after Washington signed off. Nvidia's founder came back after Washington weighed in.

Meanwhile the two worlds are tied together by money. When Anthropic went public, Nvidia and Alphabet ($GOOGL), the parent of Google, each bought $10 billion of Anthropic stock in a $26 billion private sale that closed alongside the IPO on November 20.

The biggest champion of open models in America now holds that stake in the closed lab that Lutnick proved he can switch off.

WHAT THE SWITCH MEANS FOR YOU

A closed model is a service. The company runs it on its own servers, and one cabinet officer can order it off for every customer.

An open-weight model on your own machine answers to you. Nobody in Washington can send it a letter.

text:
OpenAI has finally released its first open-weight large language models since 2019’s GPT-2. These new “gpt-oss” models are available in two different sizes and score similarly to the company’s o3-mini and o4-mini models on several benchmarks. Unlike the models available through OpenAI’s web interface, these new open models can be freely downloaded, run, and even modified on laptops and other local devices.

In the company’s many years without an open LLM release, some users have taken to referring to it with the pejorative “ClosedAI.” That sense of frustration had escalated in the past few months as these long-awaited models were delayed twice—first in June and then in July. With their release, however, OpenAI is reestablishing itself as a presence for users of open models.

That’s particularly notable at a time when Meta, which had previously dominated the American open-model landscape with its Llama models, may be reorienting toward closed releases—and when Chinese open models, such as DeepSeek’s offerings, Kimi K2, and Alibaba’s Qwen series, are becoming more popular than their American competitors.

“The vast majority of our [enterprise and startup] customers are already using a lot of open models,” said Casey Dvorak, a research program manager at OpenAI, in a media briefing about the model release. “Because there is no [competitive] open model from OpenAI, we wanted to plug that gap and actually allow them to use our technology across the board.”

The new models come in two different sizes, the smaller of which can theoretically run on 16 GB of RAM—the minimum amount that Apple currently offers on its computers. The larger model requires a high-end laptop or specialized hardware.

Open models have a few key use cases. Some organizations may want to customize models for their own purposes or save money by running models on their own equipment, though that equipment comes at a substantial upfront cost. Others—such hospitals, law firms, and governments—might need models that they can run locally for data security reasons. 

OpenAI has facilitated such activity by releasing its open models under a permissive Apache 2.0 license, which allows the models to be used for commercial purposes. Nathan Lambert, post-training lead at the Allen Institute for AI, says that this choice is commendable: Such licenses are typical for Chinese open-model releases, but Meta released its Llama models under a bespoke, more restrictive license. “It’s a very good thing for the open community,” he says.

Researchers who study how LLMs work also need open models, so that they can examine and manipulate those models in detail. “In part, this is about reasserting OpenAI’s dominance in the research ecosystem,” says Peter Henderson, an assistant professor at Princeton University who has worked extensively with open models. If researchers do adopt gpt-oss as new workhorses, OpenAI could see some concrete benefits, Henderson says—it might adopt innovations discovered by other researchers into its own model ecosystem.

More broadly, Lambert says, releasing an open model now could help OpenAI reestablish its status in an increasingly crowded AI environment. “It kind of goes back to years ago, where they were seen as the AI company,” he says. Users who want to use open models will now have the option to meet all their needs with OpenAI products, rather than turning to Meta’s Llama or Alibaba’s Qwen when they need to run something locally.

The rise of Chinese open models like Qwen over the past year may have been a particularly salient factor in OpenAI’s calculus. An employee from OpenAI emphasized at the media briefing that the company doesn’t see these open models as a response to actions taken by any other AI company, but OpenAI is clearly attuned to the geopolitical implications of China’s open-model dominance. “Broad access to these capable open-weights models created in the US helps expand democratic AI rails,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the models’ release. 

Since DeepSeek exploded onto the AI scene at the start of 2025, observers have noted that Chinese models often refuse to speak about topics that the Chinese Communist Party has deemed verboten, such as Tiananmen Square. Such observations—as well as longer-term risks, like the possibility that agentic models could purposefully write vulnerable code—have made some AI experts concerned about the growing adoption of Chinese models. “Open models are a form of soft power,” Henderson says.

Lambert released a report on Monday documenting how Chinese models are overtaking American offerings like Llama and advocating for a renewed commitment to domestic open models. Several prominent AI researchers and entrepreneurs, such as HuggingFace CEO Clement Delangue, Stanford’s Percy Liang, and former OpenAI researcher Miles Brundage, have signed on.

The Trump administration, too, has emphasized development of open models in its AI Action Plan. With both this model release and previous statements, OpenAI is aligning itself with that stance. “In their filings about the action plan, [OpenAI] pretty clearly indicated that they see US–China as a key issue and want to position themselves as very important to the US system,” says Rishi Bommasani, a senior research scholar at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. 

And OpenAI may see concrete political advantages from aligning with the administration’s AI priorities, Lambert says. As the company continues to build out its extensive computational infrastructure, it will need political support and approvals, and sympathetic leadership could go a long way.
